common_name: Chocolate White Snakeroot (Dark-Leaved Native Woodland Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chocolate is a dark-foliaged selection of the native white snakeroot, valued as much for its purple-bronze leaves as for its late-season flowers.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection tolerates deep shade and dry soil once established better than most dark-foliaged perennials, which are more often bred for sun. Chocolate carries rich, glossy, purple-bronze foliage through the growing season, deepest in color with some morning sun, then tops out in late summer to fall with airy, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that draw a heavy late-season crush of bees and butterflies when few other shade plants are blooming. It self-seeds readily, and while the straight species is a valuable native, all parts of white snakeroot are toxic to livestock and were historically responsible for fatal 'milk sickness' in humans who drank milk from cows that had grazed it, so keep it out of pastures and away from grazing animals. Deadhead spent flower heads if self-seeding becomes excessive, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Native Plant Trials

common_name: Golden Jubilee Anise Hyssop (Golden-Leaved Licorice-Scented Herb)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or transplant divisions in spring, into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Golden Jubilee was an All-America Selections winner for its bright chartreuse-gold foliage that holds color all season.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; good drainage matters more than fertility, since wet winter soil is the most common cause of loss. Golden Jubilee is an All-America Selections-winning form of anise hyssop grown as much for its bright, licorice-scented chartreuse-to-gold foliage, which holds its color from spring through fall, as for its lavender-blue flower spikes that appear from midsummer into fall and draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in steady numbers. The aromatic leaves can be used fresh or dried for tea and as an anise-flavored culinary herb, much like the green-leaved species. It self-seeds modestly in favorable conditions, tolerates drought well once established, and needs little more than a spring cutback of old growth and an occasional deadheading to tidy the plant and extend bloom.

common_name: Kudos Mandarin Agastache (Compact Orange Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Transplant out after the danger of frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Kudos Mandarin is a compact, heavy-blooming hummingbird mint bred by Terra Nova Nurseries for a tidy, floriferous habit.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, since this hummingbird mint is far more prone to winter rot in heavy, wet soil than to any problem from summer drought. Kudos Mandarin forms a compact, densely branched mound of aromatic foliage covered from early summer to frost in tightly packed spikes of warm orange flowers, blooming from the base of the plant to the tip rather than thinning out partway up the spike as many older agastache cultivars do, and it draws hummingbirds and bees in steady numbers all season. Its tidy, well-branched habit needs no staking and holds up well through summer storms. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter just before new growth resumes, and avoid winter mulch piled against the crown, which encourages rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Voodoo is among the darkest-colored of the creeping stonecrops, holding deep burgundy-red foliage color all season rather than just in cool weather.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; standing winter moisture, not cold, is what kills this drought-proof succulent groundcover. Voodoo forms a dense, low mat of tiny, fleshy, deep burgundy-red leaves that hold their rich color through the growing season and intensify further in cool fall weather, topped in summer by flat clusters of small, star-shaped pink flowers that draw bees and small butterflies. Its low, spreading habit fills rock garden pockets, green roof plantings, and hot, dry slopes where little else thrives, tolerating poor, gravelly soil and reflected heat from pavement without complaint. It needs essentially no maintenance beyond an occasional trim to keep it within bounds and division every several years if a mat becomes bare in the center.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Coral Carpet Sedum (Fine-Textured Bronze-Red Groundcover Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Coral Carpet forms an extremely low, fine-textured mat that colors bronze-red in full sun and cool weather, greening somewhat in shade or high summer heat.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, even gravelly soil in full sun; this creeping stonecrop is one of the lowest-growing groundcover sedums available, forming a dense carpet barely two to three inches tall studded with tiny, bead-like leaves that shift from bronze-green in summer to a richer coral-red in full sun and cool weather. Clusters of small white starry flowers appear in early summer, but the fine, mossy foliage texture is the main draw, making it useful for planting between stepping stones, along the edges of dry rock gardens, or as a low-water lawn substitute on a small scale. It tolerates foot traffic better than most sedums but resents standing water and heavy, poorly drained soil, which quickly cause rot. It requires no fertilizing and spreads readily from small broken-off pieces that root wherever they touch soil, so division and propagation are essentially effortless.
